opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, what surprised me most was how *semantically consistent* the latent actions turned out to be. Remember, we never gave the model any action labels. It just watched a huge amount of internet video of 2D platformer games and had to infer, frame to frame, what "action" could explain the change. We constrained it to a very small discrete set, eight latent actions, partly so a human could actually play with it.

You'd expect it to pick up left and right, since that's the dominant motion in those games. But it also learned things like jumping, and not just "move the sprite up." The character goes up, arcs, and comes back down, so there's an implicit sense of physics tied to that one latent code. And the same latent action meant the same thing across very different contexts. Press the "jump" code in one world, then in a completely different art style, even in a child's sketch or a real photograph we prompted it with, and the character would still jump. That generalization to out-of-distribution images was really exciting to me.

There were also subtler emergent behaviors. In some generations you'd see parallax, where background layers move at different speeds as the character moves, which is a learned notion of depth. We saw hints of deformable objects and other elements of the scene responding to the character, not just the character itself moving.

What I find compelling is that it suggests you can extract a controllable, action-conditioned world model purely from passive observation. That's a big deal if you care about training agents, because most of the world's video doesn't come with actions attached. If a model can discover a meaningful action space on its own, that opens up a lot of possibilities for learning behaviors from video at scale.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so the directional stuff — left, right, jump — that's kind of what you'd expect to fall out of a model trained on platformer videos. What really surprised us was that Genie picked up on things we hadn't explicitly set out to capture. One of the latent actions ended up corresponding to something like a "do nothing" or stay-still action, which is actually really important for game control — you need the ability to not move. We also saw actions that seemed to map onto interactions with the environment rather than just moving the character, like things that would trigger a change in the scene.

And the part I found most interesting is that these actions were consistent across completely different images. So the same latent action that made the character jump in one game would make a character jump in a totally different game, or even in a hand-drawn sketch or a real-world photo we fed in. That consistency is what tells you the model has learned something about the structure of control, not just memorized frame transitions. We only had eight latent actions, so the model had to be pretty economical about what it chose to represent, and it's striking that it carved up the space in a way that lines up so well with how a human would think about controlling a game.

astra-6.text: What stood out to me was that it learned a jump action without being explicitly told what jumping was. It was learning from videos, without action labels, and still discovered a distinction between moving left or right and jumping. And those actions were consistent across different scenes, so you could use the same action to control a character in a new environment. That’s a really interesting step beyond simply predicting what the next frame should look like.
